entities.description: The Fool as rendered across the four supported decks. In the Tarot de Marseille he is Le Mat — the unnumbered wanderer outside the sequence. Thoth retains the name and Crowley's imagery of the Green Man. Etteilla retained the Fool at the liminal boundary of his numbered sequence, labelling it both 0 and 78, and read it as folly, madness, and the unchecked mind unmoored from reason. Card 1 in Etteilla's deck ('Etteilla — The Questioner') is a separate self-card unique to his system, not a replacement for the Fool.

The Magician (I) across four decks. TdM names him Le Bateleur — the street conjurer. Thoth renames him The Magus, emphasising his role as divine Word and mediator of will. Etteilla retains The Magician.

The High Priestess (II) across four decks. TdM names her La Papesse — the female Pope, evoking the legend of Pope Joan. Thoth names her The Priestess, stripping the papal reference and centering her as pure lunar gnosis.

The Empress (III) across four decks. All four traditions render her as the fertile, enthroned mother-goddess, attributed to Venus. The name is consistent across RWS, Thoth, and Etteilla; TdM calls her La Impératrice.
The Emperor (IV) across four decks. Consistently the archetype of temporal authority, Aries, and the paternal principle. TdM names him La Emperour.

The Hierophant (V) across four decks. TdM names him Le Pape — the Pope — the spiritual authority of the Church. RWS and Etteilla use Hierophant; Thoth retains it but reframes him as initiator into the mysteries rather than ecclesiastical authority.

The Lovers (VI) across four decks. TdM calls it L'Amoureux — a young man choosing between two women — an explicit scene of moral choice. RWS shifts to Adam and Eve. Thoth elaborates into a alchemical marriage of opposites under the figure of Perseus and Andromeda.

The Chariot (VII) across four decks. Consistently the triumphant will in control of opposing forces, attributed to Cancer. All four decks depict an armoured figure driving a chariot pulled by opposing beasts or sphinxes.

Strength (XI in the traditional order; VIII in RWS and derivatives) across four decks. Waite and Smith swapped the positions of Strength and Justice from the historical sequence. Thoth renames the card Lust, refocusing it on Babalon riding the Beast — ecstatic, creative will rather than gentle restraint.
The Hermit (IX) across four decks. The solitary seeker with the lantern. All four decks are broadly consistent in imagery. Thoth adds Cerberus at his feet, emphasising mastery over the underworld.

Wheel of Fortune (X) across four decks. TdM shows La Roue de Fortune with ascending and descending figures. Thoth renames it Fortune and adds the Sphynx, Hermanubis, and Typhon, placing the Wheel in a cosmic rather than fatalistic frame.

Justice (VIII in the traditional order; XI in RWS and derivatives) across four decks. Waite and Smith swapped Justice and Strength from the historical sequence. Thoth renames the card Adjustment, shifting emphasis from legal justice to the cosmic principle of equilibrium — the Maat of the Egyptian tradition.

The Hanged Man (XII) across four decks. The suspended figure, voluntary sacrifice and reversal of perspective. TdM's Le Pendu holds bags of coins. RWS adds the halo. Thoth's figure hangs from the ankh with serpents, connecting the sacrifice to Osiris.

Death (XIII) across four decks. The skeleton and scythe of transformation. TdM's La Mort shows only the skeleton. RWS adds the mounted knight with the white rose. Thoth shows the Egyptian skeleton wielding the scythe of the New Aeon.

Temperance (XIV) across four decks. Thoth renames the card Art — the Great Work of alchemy and the union of opposites — replacing the temperance virtue with active transformation. TdM and Etteilla retain Temperance; RWS adds the angel Iris above a pool.

The Devil (XV) across four decks. Consistently the archetype of bondage, materialism, and Set or Pan. All four decks show a horned figure with chained figures. Thoth's imagery draws on Pan-Priapus and the goat of Mendes.

The Tower (XVI) across four decks. TdM names it La Maison Dieu — the House of God — a falling tower struck by lightning. Thoth retains The Tower with the Eye of Shiva destroying the old aeon. RWS adds the crown and two falling figures.

The Star (XVII) across four decks. The naked figure pouring water beneath a great star. Etteilla unusually maps two cards to this archetype: The Heavens (Card 4) represents the celestial firmament and divine cosmic order, while The Stars (Card 6) carries the more familiar Star meanings of hope, guidance, and celestial light. Thoth's Star shows Nuit, the infinite sky, arched over the cosmos.
The Moon (XVIII) across four decks. The moon, the path, the crayfish, the howling dogs or wolves. All four decks are broadly consistent. Thoth's Moon adds the Egyptian scarab rising from the waters.

The Sun (XIX) across four decks. The great luminary of vitality, consciousness, and spiritual illumination. Etteilla titles his card The Lighted Torch — The Sun. Thoth's Sun shows the Rose of Tiphareth with twin children.

Judgement (XX) across four decks. Thoth replaces the Judgement card entirely with The Aeon — the proclamation of the Thelemic Aeon of Horus supplanting the Aeon of Osiris. TdM's Le Jugement and Etteilla's The Last Judgment show the angel sounding the trumpet of resurrection.

The World (XXI) across four decks. Thoth renames it The Universe, showing Nuit arched over the cosmic globe with the Fool descending into matter. TdM's Le Monde and RWS show a dancing figure within a laurel wreath.
